title: Mercedes SLK R170: hydraulic roof leak, stained headliner and the checks to make
author: Caramagnols
excerpt: On a SLK R170, a leaking roof hose does more than leave a mark inside. It means checking the circuit, the pump and the cylinders before a comfort annoyance becomes a real failure.
content:
On our car, one hydraulic hose had already been replaced before the purchase. Yet oil was still left inside the headliner. That detail is enough to show that a retractable roof is not defined only by whether it opens or not.

A leak in the roof circuit does not threaten the interior trim alone. It also means that part of the system has aged, that pressure is escaping where it should not and that another weak point may appear if one keeps cycling the roof without a proper reading of the whole system.

A leak that goes beyond the stain

The first reflex is often to look only at the oil trace on the headliner or near the trim panels. That is understandable, but insufficient. The real question is not merely how to clean the consequence. It is why the circuit let oil out and what condition the other hoses, cylinders and fittings are now in.

On the Mercedes SLK, the retractable hardtop is part of the model’s identity. When its hydraulics start leaking, one does not lose a secondary comfort item. One weakens one of the very systems that make daily roadster use sensible.

Where to look on a R170

The first checks should cover the hoses in articulation areas, the points where the material works at every opening, then the pump, the cylinders and the boot areas that may collect less visible traces. A stained headliner is sometimes only the most readable part of an older or more diffuse leak.

The way the roof behaves also matters. Slower movement, asymmetry or hesitation do not prove a leak on their own, but they do justify stopping automatic demonstrations. On an older car, the best way to preserve a delicate system is often to stop early rather than test for too long.

When to stop operating the roof

If the roof still works but leaves oil behind, it is wiser not to multiply cycles just to show that everything still opens. Every movement restarts pressure, moves fluid and can worsen a weakness that is already there. A successful demonstration is not worth a hydraulic circuit dirtier than before.

The better compromise is one controlled opening or closing, followed by observation and then workshop diagnosis. On a SLK R170, the goal is not to impress. It is to keep a coherent and dry mechanism, reliable enough to remain pleasant in regular use.

Putting the interior right after the cause is solved

The headliner should only be repaired once the leak itself has been dealt with. Cleaning or replacing it too early often prepares a second round of damage. In our case, restoring the interior makes sense only after the faulty hose is treated and the rest of the circuit has been checked.

It is a useful method reminder for any youngtimer with a complex roof. One does not finish with the visible parts in order to forget the rest. One finishes with the visible parts once the mechanical cause is under control. Only then does the roof recover its proper role: protect, open the car when it should and stay discreet the rest of the time.

This technical reading goes with our page on bringing the SLK 230 Kompressor back to a proper standard. To see how the rest of the work should then be ordered, read also our note on the right order for putting the car back on the road after purchase.
